Discover Board Game Arena Rules summary Contents 1 Schnapsen - Quick Rules 1.1 Overview 1.2 Card Values 1.3 Gameplay 1.4 Special Actions 1.5 Scoring Schnapsen - Quick Rules Overview Players: 2 players. Deck: 20 cards (Ace, 10, King, Queen, Jack in four suits). Objective: Be the first to reach 66 card points through tricks and announcements, or win the very last trick. Card Values Ace: 11 points Ten: 10 points King: 4 points Queen: 3 points Jack: 2 points Gameplay Each player is dealt 5 cards. One card is placed face-up under the stock (Talon); its suit is the trump suit. Trick-taking: The non-dealer leads the first card. As long as the stock is not empty or "closed," there is no requirement to follow suit. The higher card of the suit led or a trump wins the trick. Drawing: After each trick, both players draw a card from the stock (winner first). Announcements (Marriages): If you hold the King and Queen of the same suit, you can announce them when leading one of them (20 points; 40 points in trumps). Points only count if the player wins at least one trick. Special Actions Exchanging (Robbing): If you hold the Trump Jack, you may swap it for the face-up trump card under the stock (if it is your turn to lead). Closing the Stock: If a player believes they can reach 66 points without drawing more cards, they can "close" the stock. From this moment on, players must follow suit and win the trick if possible. Scoring The round ends as soon as a player reaches 66 points or the last trick is taken. The winner earns game points: 3 points: If the opponent has no tricks. 2 points: If the opponent has fewer than 33 points (Schneider). 1 point: If the opponent has 33 or more points. The overall goal is to count down from 7 points to 0. [Rating: 2/10] A repetitive, luck driven card game. Used to be popular with the working-class of Hungary back during the socialism, who played this mainly in cheap, dodgy pubs for pennies. Only entertaining while drinking with your mates. I used to play this a lot as a young kid (without the booze, of course!) but only because we did not know any better.

[Rating: 2/10] traditional game of my home-country Austria. Mainly just memory and luck … but you can play it with your grand parents.

[Rating: 2.5/10] Very luck-heavy. Except for a few decisions, the game basically plays you instead of vice versa.

[Rating: 3/10] Interesting, primarily due to the different pre and post-"closing" rules, but ultimately it's 75% luck due to the tiny deck.

[Rating: 3/10] It got worse with each consecutive play, will always choose Watten instead of this

[Rating: 4/10] The two player "variant" of Bauernschnapsen.  This variant is even worse than a 3 player game of Bauernschnapsen (and that one is best with 4 players).  My personal problem is that there is a lot of randomness in this version, first of all because you get so many different cards over the course of the game and because you don't have to follow suit untill there are still cards in the facedown pile (after that one runs oit you have to follow suit). [Rating: 5/10] It's a 2 player time-passer trick taking game, similar in spirit to others where you play 1 draw 1, try and remember what's gone, can guess what the other might have picked up yet and play accordingly. Can't be taken too seriously as a result.

[Rating: 5/10] Nagy gyerekkori kedvenc, néhány időpontot tudtam csak így utólag beazonosítani, de rengetegszer játszottuk egészen a 80-as évektől napjainkig. (magyar kártya) Jó játék, de bizonyos rutin felett egysíkú, túl egyértelmű. A 4-est szeretem leginkább, a 2 személyes elég unalmas.

[Rating: 5/10] Not a fan of memory games, and this one really needs the memory element to make it distinct from others of the same ilk.

[Rating: 5/10] A two-player card game of the same general type as Briscola, with all the non-scoring cards ripped out and with some additional wrinkles. Definitely more devious, but I don't get the focus on drawing the king and queen of trumps, and there's a lot of counting of cards and points to determine when to close if you want to play well. As with many traditional card games there's a million variations in the gameplay and scoring details.

[Rating: 5/10] Ending a round by claiming to have won it is a fun mechanic. A bit too much short-term memory involved for my tastes, though.
